That means that the odds can change after you make a wager. For example, a horse might be 20-1 at the window when you place your wager, but if money rolls in late on that horse, it might be 10-1 by the time the race begins.   Because all the wagers are pooled, payout odds will be exactly the same regardless of what race book you're using.         One of the New York Yankees' franchise legends is at odds with the club. Jorge Posada, the team's stalwart catcher during the Joe Torre dynasty years, recently told the New York Post that he doesn't believe the Yankees want him to return to the club in any kind of role. Posada said: "I mean, I could, but I don't think they want me there, to tell you the truth."I don't feel welcome when I go there, you know? Even in spring training, I don't feel like -- I'm just like, I don't know, I don't feel welcome. I don't feel like they want me there, so I don't go."Posada, a four-time World Series champion with New York, did not elaborate on his comments or cite a specific incident that made him feel unwelcome in the organization. Posada, now 56, first signed with the Yankees after they made him a 24th-round pick in 1990. He spent his entire professional career in pinstripes. Posada's MLB career with the Yankees lasted from 1995 through 2011. Over that span, he compiled 1,664 hits, 275 home runs, 936 walks, 1,065 RBI and a WAR of 42.7. Along the way, Posada earned five All-Star selections as the Yankees' primary catcher and twice finished in the top 10 of the American League MVP vote. In 2015, the Yankees retired Posada's No. 20. Since retiring as a player, Posada has held a number of baseball jobs, including a front office role with the Miami Marlins when his former Yankees teammate Derek Jeter was atop the club's front office.

title: Inside North Carolina's GM search: How Bill Belichick could reshape UNC's future - CBS Sports

body:
As Belichick navigates Year 2 at UNC, the program's next GM will help shape roster strategy, leadership structure and long-term direction
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 28, 2026

    12:44 pm ET

        On July 27, North Carolina suspended college football's highest-paid general manager, Michael Lombardi, from his post, citing an HR investigation. He was head coach Bill Belichick's handpicked GM and his initial hire.The GM role has been handled effectively by Belichick, according to sources with knowledge of the program's management structure since then (Lombardi officially resigned in early September). But that will change soon, as the search for a general manager eventually comes to a close. The Tar Heels sit at 4-3 with two close losses. Those around the program acknowledge that the team has improved. A bowl game is highly likely but not guaranteed; however, the Tar Heels did not hire an eight-time Super Bowl champion to scrape by to .500, as the program has been almost exactly that since 2000 (165-167). UNC's 2027 recruiting class currently has 16 commitments, which is not an abnormal number at this point in the cycle, and a new GM is expected to be tasked with navigating the transfer portal, which officially opens in January, and retaining the current roster.
Former Michigan GM Sean Magee is consulting with the football program as his firm, TurnkeyZRG, leads the search for a permanent GM. That GM is not expected to be in place before the end of the regular season, according to a source with knowledge of the search process. 
        
            
                Lincoln Riley, Deion Sanders and Kyle Whittingham: Inside the jobs that could shake up the coaching carousel
                
                    John Talty                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
How will UNC structure the new GM's role?There is a chance that UNC will adopt a model in which the GM reports to athletic director Steve Newmark and to Belichick. Lombardi reported solely to Belichick, according to a copy of his original employment letter obtained by CBS Sports. The model is en vogue in college football as a wave of professionalization sweeps across the sport. It is notably different from how Belichick handled business for years in the NFL when he served as what the league defined as the "primary football executive" for the New England Patriots, essentially meaning he was the de facto general manager, although he did not formally hold the title with the team. 
In 2024, when Belichick was in the mix for the Atlanta Falcons job, team owner Arthur Blank squashed the notion that Belichick would want to be the team's GM, saying that in a text, Belichick had conveyed he was willing to work with then-GM Terry Fontenot. The NFL had long since moved away from the model of the head coach as the primary roster decision-maker, and Belichick was among the last of that dying breed with New England. As the amount of money on college football rosters increases (Belichick's contract guarantees at least $20 million in roster spending), the need for a GM to have some autonomy becomes more important. UNC has an opportunity to continue a growing trend. Florida, Oklahoma, Stanford and California have varying versions of an empowered GM. Whoever is atop UNC football will also always have to contend with the fact that UNC men's basketball is a massive priority at the school, and new head coach Mike Malone's roster is in the $20 million club, according to CBS Sports' Matt Norlander, which puts it near the top of the sport. Football is the primary economic driver of an athletic department, however, even at a place like UNC.
An industry source wondered whether Belichick preferred to go with someone with NFL experience. NFL personnel executives have increasingly turned their eyes toward college jobs mainly for the pay (Lombardi was making a nation-leading $1.5 million annually in base pay). But no matter how much college football looks more and more like the NFL each year, there are still elements that retain the way things used to be, mainly in the sales and hospitality roles that remain tied to the recruiting world. There is also the unavoidable nature of university-side politics, especially at a place like UNC that led to a fractured search to get Belichick in the first place, with trustees lobbying for Belichick and athletic department administrators working with conventional names. In the NFL, roster negotiations are formulaic. If a defender has X sacks, Y tackles, and Z interceptions, there are comparisons teams and agents use, then negotiate from there because everyone knows what everybody else makes. While topline roster estimates exist and individual player salaries are reported, the numbers can vary widely across athletic departments regarding how much money is actually on a team's books. There is no real salary cap (the highest-paid rosters are around $50 million in college football, although the revenue-sharing cap is around $21 million), and the extent of teeth CSC enforcement has remains to be seen.  
It's not clear who is in the mix for the general manager job, but that person's profile will be a bellwether for the short-term future. Mainly Belichick's, whose contract is no longer guaranteed after the 2027 season. Not reporting directly to Belichick alone could signal someone who will be around after he is out of the job. But Belichick is renowned for working with guys he's always been with. He and Lombardi went back to the Browns in the 1990s. His son Steve was on staff (and resigned in the wake of the same investigation that involved Lombardi), and his other son, Brian, remains on staff. Saturday, UNC puts its middle-of-the-pack ACC roster on the field against one of the nation's highest-powered teams in Miami. The future of UNC's roster will be one of the most intriguing storylines in the world of college football personnel heading into this offseason.

body:
The NBA season is underway and chaos already abounds. The Grizzlies are one of three undefeated teams atop the Western Conference; the Heat are winless and in disarray; and there has been a rash of major injuries to superstars across the league, raising countless questions about how teams go forward from here. Given all that, it's time for our overreactions from the season's first week. The basketball gods are cruel and mercilessThis isn't even an overreaction. The season has barely begun, and there's already been an endless string of serious injuries to big-name players. Anthony Edwards and Kawhi Leonard were the latest of the bunch. On Tuesday, news emerged that Edwards will undergo arthroscopic surgery on his right knee and miss up to two months. That's a huge blow for the Wolves, who were off to a 3-1 start. Now, Minnesota will have to figure out a way to stay afloat without Edwards, who was the second leading scorer in the NBA behind only Luka Dončić. Meanwhile, the Raptors will be without Leonard for "a period of weeks" while he deals with swelling in his right knee. 
        
            
                How can Timberwolves survive Anthony Edwards' absence? LaMelo Ball must level up, but there's another key
                
                    Brad Botkin                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
It continues. The Jazz will be without Jaren Jackson Jr. for six to eight weeks after he tore his MCL. The Magic lost Paolo Banchero for four to six weeks with a right ankle sprain, as well as Jalen Suggs, who will be re-evaluated in two weeks after bruising his right knee. Pistons center Jalen Duren is out at least two weeks with a hamstring strain. Kristaps Porziņģis, Kon Knueppel and AJ Dybantsa have yet to play for their respective teams due to various injuries/health issues. And after sitting out all of last season, Ben Simmons blew out his Achilles before playing a single regular-season minute for the Kings.And then there are the Thunder. Jalen Williams played just 33 games last season but returned healthy and ready to go this year -- only to suffer a dislocated ankle and a fractured fibula against the Clippers over the weekend. If you haven't seen it, don't search for it. It was the kind of gruesome scene that made many people recall the awful and unforgettable injuries previously suffered by Gordon Hayward and Paul George. The Thunder haven't officially declared Williams done for the season, but it would be surprising if he recovered from significant surgery in time to return. Oklahoma City also lost Cason Wallace with a torn labrum. Same situation there in terms of facing long odds on bouncing back from surgery in time to play this season or postseason. 
The NBA is at its most enjoyable when the brightest stars are available to shine on the court. This is a dark start. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    The Thunder are still one of the teams to beat in the West Deep breath, Thunder fans. No one wanted to see OKC lose Williams and Wallace. It was a brutal blow for the players and the team. Adding another injury to the ever-growing list, Alex Caruso -- who was expected to play increased minutes and take on more responsibility with two of the Thunder's best defenders on the mend -- made it just nine minutes into their game against the Suns before spraining his ankle. He's already listed as out for Wednesday's outing in Dallas and is expected to miss some time.It's hard to imagine a worse scenario for the Thunder, who began the season with the best odds to win the NBA title. But even with those unwelcome developments, OKC is still among the betting favorites to make a deep run this postseason. The Thunder (+380 at FanDuel) are second behind only the Spurs (+280) to win the Western Conference and the NBA Finals. That has everything to do with what Sam Presti has constructed in Oklahoma City. The Thunder are the deepest team in the league -- and now that premise will be tested. 
Ajay Mitchell -- who began the season on the shortlist for Sixth Man of the Year candidates -- will be called upon to provide a scoring boost in the absence of Williams. (Mitchell is already off to a good start there, scoring an efficient career-high 30 points in 25 minutes in a win over the Suns on Monday.) The same goes for Jared McCain, who has morphed from a luxury addition following a trade with the 76ers last season to a critical component this year. You can also imagine Mark Daigneault leaning more on his bigs with Chet Holmgren, Isaiah Hartenstein and rookie Aday Mara. Jaylin Williams and another rookie, Bennett Stirtz, will have to gobble up minutes off the bench. And as always, the whole thing revolves around Shai Gilgeous-Alexander. Losing two players as important and talented as Williams and Wallace is an unlucky and unwanted turn of events, but as long as the reigning two-time MVP is on the floor, OKC remains formidable. If any team can handle this kind of strife, it's the Thunder. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    The Knicks still have to shake off that hangoverHey, look at that: New York finally won a game. The Knicks beat the Pistons at home on Tuesday, which undoubtedly came as a relief to them and their fans. New York started the season with three duds, losing at home on ring/banner night to the Sixers, falling in Boston to the Celtics, and then faceplanting at home to a Magic team that was without Banchero. Not how they wanted to begin their title defense. The 0-3 start was the worst beginning to a follow-up season by the reigning champs since the Mavericks dropped their initial three games 15 years ago. When you win the first championship in 53 years, you can be forgiven for enjoying yourself over the summer and being distracted by the spotlight. It also probably didn't help their focus that the team paused negotiations with Karl Anthony-Towns and Josh Hart, or that the organization initially duped employees with a championship ring email that was actually a cybersecurity test (before later realizing how bad the optics are on that kind of thing and promising to retroactively make it right). 
The good news, to the extent that there is any when you only win one of your first four games, is that Towns has played well so far -- he's averaging 22.5 points and 14 rebounds on 60.3% shooting from the floor -- even while the rest of the team has been largely inconsistent. The upcoming schedule is also encouraging. Over their next seven games, the Knicks play the Bulls twice, as well as the Nets and Bucks. After that, they have a road trip featuring games in Toronto (without Kawhi) and Minnesota (sans Edwards). The Knicks still have quite a bit of work to do to return to form, but finally securing that first win did "a lot" for their psyche, as a relieved Jalen Brunson acknowledged after beating the Pistons. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    The Nuggets should be the most worriedYou know things aren't going well when your three-time former MVP picks a fight with the fans -- and then doubles down. The Nuggets are 1-2. After Denver completed a 23-point comeback to barely beat the Pelicans at home in overtime, for the team's only win of the season, Nikola Jokić called out the fans for having the audacity to call out the Nuggets.
"I think those fans that booed, they don't need to come anymore," Jokic said. "If you guys follow us, you know that we never quit and we came back from much worse for similar situations. So if they ask me, they are not welcome anymore."
Given a chance later to walk that back, Joker followed it up by saying he was sticking to his original point: "I think they are not real fans." Maybe this is an offshoot of the European soccer ethos that encourages supporters to rally behind their team when they let in a goal or get in a tough spot. Or maybe Jokić is just in his feelings about the Nuggets playing like garbage on the whole to start the season. As a native Philadelphian, it's always amusing to me when players get sore about people letting them know that they're not performing well. The easy solution is to perform better and the boos will abate. Problem solved. Unfortunately for the Nuggets and their sensitivities, they followed up that win over the Pelicans by getting smoked by 20 on their own floor by the Warriors. Not ideal. 

                            
    
                                                
                    
    Actually, the Warriors are in worse shapeYes, Golden State topped the Nuggets in Denver for its only win of the season, but that's only one more victory than the winless Pelicans and Kings have mustered. Not exactly the kind of company the Warriors want to keep. Golden State lost its opener at the Lakers, fell at home to the Grizzlies, then took another L on the road in Phoenix. Through their first four games, the Warriors were 19th in net rating and looking lost. The question is how they find their way, or if that's even possible. Rookie Yaxel Lendeborg has been one of the few bright spots in the Bay. He's second on the team in points per game behind only Steph Curry, and he leads the Warriors in rebounds per game and verbal altercations with rival MVP candidates. (That last bit is saying something considering Draymond Green is still employed by the Warriors.)The question is whether reinforcements will arrive in time to turn the Warriors into a competitive team and give them a shot at the play-in (sorry, Warriors fans but the playoffs proper look awfully far away right now). Jimmy Butler and Moses Moody are both recovering from knee injuries and it's uncertain when they might be able to return and contribute. Meanwhile, Porziņģis is reportedly contemplating his future in basketball while dealing with health concerns. It doesn't seem like the Warriors should expect any of them back anytime soon -- or, in the case of Porziņģis, who just got a new two–year contract worth $40 million -- possibly at all. 
Curry also signed a new deal this offseason: a two-year. $115 million extension. That was less than he could have demanded in order to give the Warriors increased flexibility and options to put a better team around him. He'll be 39 in March. Time is not on his side, and neither is this Warriors roster. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Check that, the Heat are in the biggest trouble Woof. The Heat are 0-4. They got blown out at home on opening night courtesy of the Wolves, then followed that up with losses to the Pistons, Hornets and Mavericks. This is obviously not what the Heat or Giannis Antetokounmpo had in mind when he left Milwaukee for South Beach. "I said what needed to be said to the media," Antetokounmpo said. "Like we all have to take a deep breath and eventually we're going to figure it out, we cannot press the panic button… It's only going to get worse if you start panicking, man. I've been in this position before. I lost five in a row, I lost seven in a row… I don't like this feeling, the moment we turn this around  -- I'm going to always remember this feeling and I'm going try to not get back to this feeling."
When your current awful start makes you recall other dreadful stretches where you dropped five or seven games in a row, you're in a bad spot. It's also not a good sign when one of your starters says exactly what Heat fans don't want to hear and had convinced themselves all offseason wouldn't be the case. After Miami acquired Antetokounmpo, critics wondered about the floor spacing and shooting around him -- or more accurately about the lack of those things given the roster construction. Just this week, Davion Mitchell underlined those very concerns, especially as they pertain to Antetokounmpo and his fit with longtime Heat fan favorite Bam Adebayo. "I think I got to do a better job of not letting [Adebayo] get lost in the game," Mitchell said after Monday's loss to Dallas. "He got to be more aggressive. I think that he will. He's still trying to figure it out because I said this before -- I think him and Giannis play in the same spaces, and then when Giannis is on the floor, he's on the floor. He can't be in those spaces."Mitchell isn't wrong. But it's not solely on Adebayo. Antetokounmpo is just as much to blame for the clunky offense. 
Adebayo admitted his shot is "not going in" at present, then complained about how "the outside noise wants to make me the scapegoat." At least he's taking this well.What was that about Giannis saying it wasn't time to press the panic button?
        
            
                Winners and losers of NBA's first week: Giannis' Heat are ice cold, OKC injuries and new-look wonders
                
                    Sam Quinn                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    

                            
    
                                                
                    
    Luka looks like an MVP frontrunnerLast week, Dončić put out an open letter to the fans, promising no excuses and no days off. Some of us were skeptical about that. Since then, Dončić has done his talking on the court. That includes the first 50-point game of the NBA season and a historic night that etched his name in the Lakers' already overpacked record book.
The oddsmakers have Victor Wembanyama as the frontrunner, followed by Gilgeous-Alexander, then Dončić. That makes sense. But Wemby started the season by publicly declaring he was overthinking things (before course correcting and feasting on the hapless Kings on Tuesday night), and SGA could very well be the latest MVP unseated by voter fatigue, even if he has another impressive season while trying to carry the injury-impacted Thunder. Imagine a scenario where Dončić keeps dropping monster numbers for a new-look Lakers team that defies expectations and finishes higher in the Western Conference standings than anyone outside of LA could have predicted. Add in the Lakers allure and if he can stack stats and wins early, he moves to the front of the line. 

                            
    
                                                
                    
    The Sixers have backup center problems that LeBron can't (or won't) solveStop me if you've heard this before. When Joel Embiid is unavailable, the Sixers don't have a good solution for the giant hole he leaves in the frontcourt. That evergreen truth was further complicated when Philly lost Ariel Hukporti to an Achilles injury before the season even began. Following that development, coach Nick Nurse rattled off a litany of names who might see some time at the five, including LeBron James. That sounded good in theory -- but not so good to James in practice. When Embiid sat the second night of a back-to-back, James started as a small-ball center in a loss to the Pistons, then explained why that wasn't a long-term fix. "Well, s--- we got an MVP over there. I'm not here to have a sustainable role at the 5," James said. "You got Joel Embiid on the team. ... If I was to say I was signed here to have a sustainable role at the 5, I don't think none of us would actually want that. I can do it, but... we have [Embiid]."They have Embiid, yes. On paper. Sometimes even on the floor. But as everyone is painfully aware, especially and including the Sixers, Embiid's availability is subject to review. He's missed 150 games over the previous three seasons. That necessitates a contingency plan. James might not want to be part of it, but extenuating circumstances sometimes force people into undesirable situations. As ever, it's something to monitor for the Sixers going forward. If they have any chance of actually competing for a championship, they'll need to stay afloat -- or at least not drown -- during the non-Embiid minutes and games. That might mean James doing something he doesn't want to do. But hey, at least James is having a good time with his new teammates. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    LeBron and Dean Wade have the best handshake in the leagueLiteral definition.

body:
The Brewers will send Jacob Misiorowski to the mound as they try again for their first championship. The Rays? We'll see
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 28, 2026
                            
                    at
    11:17 am ET
                        
                •
            
            4 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The Tampa Bay Rays took their first step toward a baseball miracle with their 12th-inning comeback win over the Milwaukee Brewers in Tuesday's Game 4 of the World Series. That 4-3 victory means the Rays avoided the sweep and cut the Brewers' series lead to 3-1. That sets the stage for Wednesday's Game 5. Tuesday's escape for the Rays was obviously an essential one, as it was an elimination game. The win also nudged the Rays' chances of winning the series from "all but impossible" to "merely a longshot." Across all of Major League Baseball postseason history, 42 teams have been down 3-0, and only one – the 2004 Boston Red Sox – has come back to win the series in question. That is, history suggests the Rays had a mere 2.4% chance of pulling off the miracle comeback when they were down 3-0. Now, though, they're down 3-1. In all, 96 teams have been down 3-1 in a best-of-seven MLB postseason series, and 14 of them have clawed back to win the series. That particular data set says the Rays have a 14.6% chance of stunning the Brewers and winning this Fall Classic. Those aren't great odds, obviously, but they're much better than the odds the Rays were facing going into Game 4. Interestingly, teams down 3-1 have a .500 record in Game 5. Speaking of which, that brings us to three questions for Game 5 – the answers to which will determine whether the Rays can cut the Brewers' advantage to 3-2 and send the series back to Milwaukee. Let's get to it.
Who's going to pitch for the Rays?Here's the big one. Rays manager Kevin Cash wisely managed Game 4 for what it was – a must-win contest. That means you worry about tomorrow when tomorrow comes and tactically do everything possible to survive the elimination game. Tomorrow, though, has now arrived, and Cash must figure out how to deploy his pitching staff for another elimination game after using seven arms on Tuesday. The most notable Game 4 decision was using Nick Martinez, who had been slated to start Game 5, in relief. Martinez worked two scoreless innings out of the bullpen and threw 33 pitches. It'll be another all-hands-on-deck affair on Wednesday, but just who those hands will be is another matter. Griffin Jax started Game 4 for Tampa Bay and amassed 74 pitches, which presumably rules him out for Game 5. As for the traditional relievers, Cole Sulser, Steven Matz, and Garrett Cleavinger did not pitch on Tuesday and thus can probably expect to be used in Game 5. Bryan Baker and Kevin Kelly did pitch in Game 4 but they didn't pitch in Monday's Game 3 blowout loss, which means they're presumably available. Ian Seymour also didn't pitch in Game 3, but his 32-pitch workload in Game 4 may rule him out. Tyler Wells and Cameron Booser have each pitched two days in a row, but desperate straits in October may mean they'll be called upon again. Is Drew Rasmussen available? He started Game 2 in Milwaukee, which means he'll be on three days of rest for Game 5. He's never made a short-rest start in his career to date. 
Given the stakes involved, anyone who's even a remotely feasible option will probably tell Cash he's willing to pitch. As such, Cash's decisions on whom to trust and whom to assign the plurality of innings will be fascinating and perhaps determinative. Will Jacob Misiorowski be in peak form?No such dilemmas are to be found for Pat Murphy and the Brewers, at least insofar as their Game 5 starter is concerned. Jacob Misiorowski, the 24-year-old NL Cy Young favorite and the hardest-throwing starting pitcher anyone's ever seen, on Wednesday will make his fourth start of these playoffs. Last time out, Misiorowski in Game 1 against the Rays went five innings and permitted only one run en route to picking up the win. "Miz" also enjoyed a velocity bump compared to his prior run of starts. 
        
            
                Jacob Misiorowski's moment? MLB's most electric starter can pitch the Brewers to their first title
                
                    Julian McWilliams                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
However, he was coming off 11 days of rest in that start, and for his Game 5 trip to the bump he'll be on the standard four days of rest. He's well into career-high-workload territory in 2026, so it remains to be seen whether the sizzle he showed in the series opener will be back for Game 5. The Brewers could use some length from him given how hard the bullpen worked in Game 4. 
Is Junior Caminero 100%?The Rays' best hitter and one of the richest power sources in all of baseball had to exit Game 4 in the 12th inning not long after reaching base on Joey Ortiz's throwing error. He did so because of an injury to his left foot. From afar, this seems like the kind of knock that would earn Caminero a few days off had it occurred in, say, June, but this is very much not June. "He'll play tomorrow on one leg," Cash said of Caminero after Game 4. "I'll make sure of it."The heart of the matter is whether Caminero will be in top form less than 24 hours after sustaining the injury. That's worth pondering in light of his ongoing power outage. Caminero this postseason has a respectable .717 OPS, but he has only one home run in 48 at-bats. That's after hitting a whopping 42 homers during the regular season and averaging one every 14.7 at-bats. It's quite possible that the Rays will need some customary thump from the hard-hitting 23-year-old if they're going to extend the series. That we shall see.

Misiorowski has been good but not his usual level of great in the playoffs ... will that change in World Series Game 5?

        ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — In the bowels of Tropicana Field early Wednesday morning, Jacob Misiorowski wouldn't even break stride.Much like his 105-mph fastball that devastates hitters and leaves observers in awe, Misiorowski moved through the crowded corridor, littered with fans, in a blur."Miz!" one fan yelled, reaching for a fist bump.But Misiorowski never extended his hand. His acknowledgment came in the form of a head nod, his attention seemingly fixed on what awaited him later that evening.For Misiorowski will take the mound Wednesday night with a chance to clinch Milwaukee's first World Series championship.
The Brewers squandered their first opportunity at history in Game 4, when Tampa Bay's Ben Williamson delivered a walk-off single in the bottom of the 12th inning. Williamson's chopper capped a two-run Rays' rally that erased Milwaukee's one-run lead and forced Wednesday's Game 5."When you're achieving something like this, it's going to have its adversity," manager Pat Murphy said. "We had some things go our way yesterday. They had some things go their way today. That's the way it is. You just live with it, and if you're a competitor, you wake up tomorrow morning and come ready to play." Isn't this what the Fall Classic is about?Letting superstars be superstars? Giving them the stage to carry their teams to baseball's ultimate glory?
Milwaukee's Cooper Pratt nearly authored his own piece of history Tuesday night. His solo home run off Ian Seymour in the top of the 12th had all the makings of a storybook ending. A rookie. Just 22 years old. Delivering on his promise six months after signing a contract extension.Pratt's night, which included three other hits, showed that the bonds holding this Brewers club together aren't rooted solely in veteran leaders like Christian Yelich and William Contreras. Or in Murphy and Milwaukee's relentless approach to the game. But also in a rookie who has enjoyed success while enduring his share of defensive growing pains.This Brewers club is the sum of its parts.Misiorowski is the Brewers' brightest star. One of the most unique starters the game has ever seen, it's all but certain he will win the NL Cy Young Award in a few weeks.
But throughout Milwaukee's dominant eight-game winning streak this October, finally snapped by Tampa Bay, Misiorowski's impact has amounted to little more than a fist bump when compared with the firm handshake of his teammates.His impact hasn't truly been felt. His dominance hasn't fully manifested.His first postseason start, against the Padres in the NLDS, lasted just four innings. His second, against the Dodgers, went only 4⅓. He was better in Game 1 of the World Series, lasting five innings. But now it's time for a Cy Young-caliber performance.And with a championship hanging in the balance, the Brewers are handing him the baseball.

That's what happens when you're down 3-0 in the World Series. Desperation mounts with each passing inning, particularly when the game hangs in the balance.Manager Kevin Cash turned to Nick Martinez, his scheduled starter for Wednesday evening. He burned through closer Bryan Baker for two innings and Ian Seymour for another. Cameron Booser recorded just one out in his second consecutive appearance.

The Brewers, meanwhile, could have gone for the kill.Aaron Ashby worked 2⅓ scoreless innings beginning in the ninth, continuing his marvelous postseason. But when Murphy removed him with one out in the 11th, it became clear that Milwaukee's manager wasn't willing to sacrifice tomorrow for today."I had an idea of why he was coming out to get me," he said. "He saw my last fastball, and I knew that was going to be on their mind."Murphy elaborated."He was disappointed he was coming out," he said. "But I said we've got to be mindful of your health, and we've got to be mindful of winning the whole thing. If you're going to win the whole thing, you have to understand that we can't drain you today or risk injury today. He's thrown a lot."Murphy never considered bringing in Misiorowski. Not in that situation. The risk was too great."You can't blow that type of situation on a one-run lead on the road," Murphy continued. "If we were in the 13th inning and we had a three-run lead, that might have been a little bit different. Probably still wouldn't have."So, on to Game 5.From the start. Where Misiorowski belongs.With the world watching. With Milwaukee's first World Series championship within reach. And with the baseball in the hands of the Brewers' 24-year-old superstar.For much of this postseason, Misiorowski has remained in the background.His dominance hasn't fully manifested. Now it's time for his moment."That loss stinks," Ashby said. "But it's part of our story. I think the boys are fired up to get back in there Wednesday."Misiorowski appeared to be.And surely, that fan would rather celebrate a World Series championship delivered by Misiorowski than receive a fist bump from him.

title: Women's college basketball is back -- and these were the offseason's biggest winners and losers - CBS Sports
description: Before the 2026-27 season tips off on Sunday, let's take a look back at the biggest offseason storylines
body:
Before the 2026-27 season tips off on Sunday, let's take a look back at the biggest offseason storylines
        
        
                                                                                                            
                                                    By
                                                
                                                            CBS Sports Staff
                                                    
                    
                                    
        
    Oct 28, 2026
                            
                    at
    11:30 am ET
                        
                •
            
            7 min read
            
        
    
            
    
        With the women's college basketball season set to tip off on Sunday (Nov. 1), it's worth taking a look at some of the major events of the summer and what programs benefited -- or didn't -- from the offseason. When we last left the sport, UCLA had just routed South Carolina to win the national championship. All six players who scored for UCLA in the Bruins' first even NCAA national title have graduated, but players such as Sienna Betts are embracing bigger roles and showing that the reigning national champions can still be competitive this upcoming season. Meanwhile, USC is preparing for a bounce-back year with the return of superstar JuJu Watkins. On the opposite side of the country, Dawn Staley's South Carolina Gamecocks are looking like a favorite even after the departure of their starting point guard Raven Johnson. Other programs are still figuring some things out, including the Tennessee Lady Vols, who had a complete roster turnover. Without further ado, here are the winners and losers of the offseason. 

                            
    
                                                
                    
    Winner: JuJu Watkins' returnThe Trojans faced some struggles during their 2025-26 campaign without star player JuJu Watkins. She tore her ACL during the second round of the 2025 NCAA Tournament, but finally made her return to practice this summer. When the season tips off in November, she will have been out for about 19 months. There might be some rust, but this is the same player who set the NCAA Division I women's basketball freshman scoring record with 920 points during the 2023-24 season. As a sophomore, she averaged 23.9 points, 6.8 rebounds, 3.4 assists, 2.2 steals and 1.8 blocks per game. Despite ending her sophomore campaign with an injury, she still earned the 2024-25 Naismith Player of the Year award. Having Watkins back is great news for USC, but what will truly make the Trojans dangerous is that she will play alongside Jazzy Davidson, who led USC in every major category last season and was named the 2025-26 national freshman of the year. The high-profile freshman streak continues this season as Coach Lindsay Gottlieb added Saniyah Hall, the No. 1 player in the ESPN class of 2026.

                            
    
                                                
                    
    Loser: Michigan's starting point guard gets injuredMichigan made the top five of our way-too-early power rankings in April because after a historic season with 28 wins and an Elite Eight appearance, the Wolverines were returning most of their key players, including Olivia Olson, Syla Swords, Mila Holloway and Te'Yala Delfosse. Unfortunately, Holloway -- the team's starting point guard for the past two seasons -- is out indefinitely due to a left lower leg injury, the team announced on Sept. 3. While no details of the injury were disclosed, it is not a torn ALC and she is expected to return to the court at some point during the season. The 5-foot-10 rising junior averaged 12.3 points, 4.1 rebounds, 4.8 assists and 1.5 steals in 28.8 minutes per game last season and was an All-Big Ten honorable mention selection. Fortunately for Michigan, coach Kim Barnes added depth to the point guard position this summer with the signing of 22-year-old Dallas Loughridge, who has professional experience that most recently includes the NBL1 South in Australia. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Winner: Oklahoma State dominated the transfer portalOklahoma State won the transfer portal this offseason with the signing of former Iowa State star Audi Crooks and former Gator Liv McGill. In January, Crooks made the CBS Sports mid-season top 10 players list because of her impressive efficiency as she was averaging 29.5 points in 26.1 minutes per game with Iowa State at the time of the rankings. Meanwhile, McGill averaged 22.5 points per contest at Florida as a crafty and athletic playmaker. 
While top transfers don't guarantee a championship, the Sooners are definitely in a better position now for a deeper NCAA Tournament run. "I think the beautiful thing about both of those players is they just want to win, and that's the number one priority for them, [and] for the rest of the team that we have," coach Jacie Hoyt told the IX Sports in August.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Loser: Lots of unknowns for TennesseeTennessee's complete roster turnover fell into the "Loser" category after the transfer portal closed in April because every player who saw the court last season either graduated or transferred. Even five-star incoming freshman Oliviyah Edwards de-committed from the program and chose South Carolina instead.
Having a completely new roster is difficult enough, but injuries have compounded Tennessee's struggles. The team signed All-Big Ten guard Kaylene Smikle, but she only played seven games during her senior season at Maryland because of knee surgery. Another promising signing was Avery Mills, a Liberty transfer who ranked No. 2 nationally with 3.1 three-pointers made per game last season. Unfortunately, Mills will be out for "an extended period" after she suffered a torn ACL and meniscus in her right knee in late June. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Winner: Class of 2022 ruling benefits South CarolinaThe Gamecocks lost some key players to graduation, including starting point guard Raven Johnson. Although replacing her was going to be difficult, the team was setting up rising junior Maddy McDaniel to step into a bigger role. However, McDaniel withdrew from the university this summer to work on her mental health, leaving the team without a true point guard on the roster. Definitely not an ideal situation, but coach Dawn Staley figured it out. Thanks to the California ruling on Aug. 18, South Carolina was able to sign fifth-year guard Brooke Quarles-Daniels, who spent two years as the starting point guard at Oakland University and then spent two seasons at Michigan -- although playing a different role more focused on defense. Despite not running the point recently, the 5-foot-7 guard still has much-needed experience in that position and Staley said other Gamecocks are willing to step up and handle some of the responsibilities. 
As a whole, South Carolina is still looking like the most dangerous team this season with the returns of Joyce Edwards and Tessa Johnson, as well as Chloe Kitts and Ashlyn Watkins, who both missed the 2025-26 season. The team also got stronger with the addition of former Texas guard Jordan Lee.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Loser: LSU's handling of the Kate Koval situationUkrainian center Kate Koval left LSU in August after the Tigers signed Russian player Anna Minaeva, because she did not feel comfortable playing with a Russian player given the ongoing war."For me, this war is not distant or abstract," Koval said on social media when explaining her decision to leave. "People close to me have been killed and wounded in Russian attacks, and places where I grew up and first began playing basketball have been destroyed by missile strikes." 
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and the two countries are still at war. While a 17-year-old player should not be blamed for the war, the situation is still a very uncomfortable one for Koval, whose father works as a drone operator for the Ukrainian military. Kim Mulkey did give Koval a heads up when the LSU coaching staff started recruiting Minerva and even suggested the two players could maybe even be ambassadors for their countries. However, Koval was still not comfortable and decided to leave despite the transfer portal already being closed. A bright spot to this story is that the NCAA granted her a waiver to transfer and Koval has officially joined Baylor. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Winner: Don't sleep on UCLA's rebuildUCLA won the 2026 NCAA Tournament but every single player who scored in the championship game has graduated, setting the team up for a major rebuild. However, the Bruins showed this summer that they are not going to fall off the map. UCLA coach Cori Close was active in the transfer portal, adding former Iowa State forward Addy Brown, former TCU guard Donovyn Hunter, former Notre Dame guard KK Bransford, former Arkansas guard Bonnie Deas and former UNC point guard Elina Aarnisalo, who actually started her college career at UCLA.
The Bruins have looked good this summer. There were a lot of bright spots in the game against Canada in July, particularly rising sophomore Sienna Betts who registered 20 points and 12 rebounds. While her sister, Lauren, has been the leader of this team for the past few years, Sienna is ready to build her own legacy. Meanwhile, the team has also gotten veteran leadership from fifth-year player Timea Gardiner, who sat out last season due to a knee injury but was a key part of UCLA's Final Four run in 2025. Recently, Close said Gardiner is seen as "the one who holds the pulse of the team." When she was spending time with freshmen Lina Jerković and Somto Okafor, both told Close that Gardiner and Hunter immediately earned their respect with how they handle themselves and their experiences with deep runs in the NCAA Tournament.Although it is hard to fully know what to expect with UCLA after losing six seniors, it seems this rebuild is heading in the right direction.

schema.headline: Women's college basketball is back -- and these were the offseason's biggest winners and losers - CBS Sports

title: Who is Christian Mbilli? Get to know the fighter ready to face Canelo Alvarez - CBS Sports
description: The 31-year-old carries knockout power and his size could pose a problem for Alvarez
body:
The 31-year-old carries knockout power and his size could pose a problem for Alvarez
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 28, 2026
                            
                    at
    1:20 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            3 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        On Saturday, Christian Mbilli will receive the biggest opportunity of his career when he steps in the ring to defend his WBC super middleweight championship against Saul "Canelo" Alvarez. While Mbilli has yet to taste defeat as a professional, the oddsmakers are favoring Alvarez, who has firmly cemented himself as a first-ballot Hall of Famer.Mbilli was the beneficiary of Alvarez's most recent fight, a loss to Terence Crawford in September 2025. After Crawford's decision to retire following a career-best victory, Mbilli was elevated from interim to full champion.Mbilli won the interim belt two fights ago, knocking out Maciej Sulecki in the first round of their June 2025 meeting. In his final fight before being elevated to full champion, Mbilli battled to a hard-fought split draw against Lester Martinez.What are Mbilli's strengths?Mbilli is a bruiser with a high-pressure style. He's muscular and strong and that allows him to bully many fighters. Of his 29 career victories, 24 have come via knockout, which speaks to his ability to turn his pressure into finishing power.
Mbilli's forward style benefits when he can back opponents toward the ropes. With an opponent trapped, Mbilli will look to throw thudding right hands to the head while also keeping a focus on throwing nasty left hands to the body, which can break opponents down if Mbilli's power doesn't catch them with a knockout shot up top.It took just 40 seconds for Mbilli to finish Mark Heffron with a body shot in their fight.Mbilli also benefits from a willingness to dirty it up in the ring. There are very few comfortable moments when Mbilli is on his game.
What are Mbilli's weaknesses?The downside to Mbilli's style is twofold, and both were on display in his draw with Martinez, a fight where he'd built up a strong early lead.Mbilli throws a lot of punches (78 per round over his five most recent fights), and a lot of them are power shots (58 per round). The power output is twice the super middleweight average, but it can lead to Mbilli fatiguing as the fight wears on. He carries a lot of muscle, which combines with his high-output style to put a lot of stress on his body, and that showed in a 10-round fight with Martinez.Mbilli also leaves himself open to counters in pursuit of big power punches. Those openings become even bigger as Mbilli fatigues.
Even when fighting with effectively one arm after suffering an injury early in the fight, Sergiy Derevyanchenko was able to find some big counters through the mid and late rounds against Mbilli.
How can Mbilli defeat Alvarez?The oddsmakers have Mbilli a +250 underdog heading into Saturday, which is certainly closer than the fight would have been seen even a year or two ago.Alvarez has gone eight fights without scoring a stoppage, which is something of a red flag for an aging fighter whose power had previously been a key factor in his fights. He does have enough pop to hurt any fighter if he lands clean, and as noted, Mbilli leaves openings for opponents to land heavy counters.
Still, the path to victory for Mbilli is fairly clear. He's a bigger man than Alvarez and thrives when he can be the bully in the ring. Alvarez isn't a high-output offensive fighter, so Mbilli has the chance to force Alvarez into an uncomfortable brawl, pushing the pace and trying to outwork his more technically gifted opponent.As Terence Crawford told DAZN, "Styles make fights, and Mbilli's style is tailor-made for Canelo. Mbilli can't do nothing but press Canelo. I don't see him beating Canelo in a boxing match. I think his best success will be letting his hands go, roughing Canelo up, and making it a dogfight."

He’ll now face the Magic, who under a new coaching regime, don’t profile as quite the spot-up shooting averse defense as they’ve been in the past. Walter cleared this line in 58% of games with 26+ minutes last season, and 72% with 28+ minutes. There is significant value at these odds.
